title: Body & health
goal: Name parts of the body, say what hurts and what's wrong, understand a doctor's advice, and say what someone should do.
intro:
When something hurts, Pashto often makes the **body part** the subject: 'my head is hurting' (سر مې خوږېږي) or 'my head does pain' (سر مې درد کوي) rather than 'I have a headache'. The little clitic مې 'my' does a lot of the work.

In this unit you'll learn body and health words, how to describe symptoms, and how to say 'should / must' with **بايد**.

vocab.note: m. Also 'mood, courage' — زړه مې غواړي 'I feel like (it)'.
f. روغه. روغ رمټ 'safe and sound'.
m/f. A female doctor: ډاکټره ḍākṭára.
Never changes; followed by the subjunctive.

phrases.en: I have a headache. (lit. my head does pain)

phrases.native: دا درمل ورځ کې درې ځله وخوره.
phrases.roman: dā darmál wradz ke dre dzála wə́xwra.
phrases.en: Take this medicine three times a day.

grammar.title: 'My head hurts': the body part as subject
grammar.body:
In Pashto the aching body part is usually the **subject**, and the person is shown by a possessive clitic (مې me, دې de, يې ye, مو mo) in second position:

سر **مې** خوږېږي 'my head is hurting' (lit. head-my hurts)
ملا **يې** درد کوي 'his back hurts' (lit. back-his pain does)

The verb agrees with the body part: پښې مې خوږېږي 'my feet hurt' (plural, same form -i). For illnesses, use **لرل** 'to have' (تبه لرم 'I have a fever') or the past participle **شوی / شوې** 'having become' (زکام شوی يم 'I've got a cold'). To ask what's wrong: **څه شوي دي؟** or **څه دې کېږي؟** (what's happening to you?).

examples.en: She is ill — she has a fever.

grammar.title: 'Should, must': بايد + subjunctive
grammar.body:
**بايد** (bāyád) means 'must / should' and never changes. It is followed by the verb in the **subjunctive** — for most verbs this is the **perfective present**, made with the stressed prefix **wə́-** plus the present endings:

زه بايد استراحت **وکړم** 'I must rest'
ته بايد درمل **وخورې** 'you should take (lit. eat) medicine'

Some verbs form the perfective differently: تلل 'go' → **لاړ شم**, راتلل 'come' → **راشم**, کېدل 'become' → **شم**. For 'shouldn't' put نه between the prefix and the verb, where it takes the stress: بايد ونه خورې (wənə́ xwre) 'you shouldn't eat (it)'. (The perfective appears in full in unit 10.)

examples.native: ته بايد ډاکټر ته لاړ شې.
examples.roman: tə bāyád ḍākṭár ta lāṛ she.
examples.en: You should go to the doctor.
I have to take this medicine.
The child should drink a lot of water.

dialogue.title: At the clinic
dialogue.setting: Gul Bibi brings her son Sami to a doctor in Mardan.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: السلام عليکم، ادې. څه شوي دي؟
lines.roman: assalā́mu ʿaláykum, adé. tsə shə́wi di?

lines.speaker: Gul Bibi
lines.native: ډاکټر صاحب، زما زوی ناروغ دی. تبه لري او ټوخی هم لري.
lines.roman: ḍākṭár sāhíb, zmā zoy nāróġ day. tabə́ lári aw ṭúxay ham lári.
lines.en: Doctor, my son is ill. He has a fever and a cough too.

lines.speaker: Sami
lines.native: هو، او سر مې هم خوږېږي.
lines.roman: ho, aw sar me ham xwaẓéẓi.
lines.en: Yes, and my head hurts too.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: How many days has it been?

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: زکام دی، ډېره د وېرې خبره نه ده. دا درمل ورځ کې درې ځله ورکړئ.
lines.roman: zukā́m day, ḍéra də wére xabə́ra na da. dā darmál wradz ke dre dzála wárkṛəy.
lines.en: It's a cold, nothing to be very worried about. Give him this medicine three times a day.

lines.speaker: Gul Bibi
lines.en: Good. What else should we do?

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: بايد استراحت وکړي او ګرمې اوبه وڅښي. ښوونځي ته دې دوه ورځې نه ځي.
lines.roman: bāyád istirāhát wə́kṛi aw gárme obə́ wə́tsṣi. ṣowundzí ta de dwa wradzé na dzi.
lines.en: He should rest and drink warm water. He shouldn't go to school for two days.

lines.speaker: Gul Bibi
lines.native: ډېره مننه، ډاکټر صاحب. خدای دې خوشاله ساتي.
lines.roman: ḍéra manə́na, ḍākṭár sāhíb. xudā́y de xoshā́la sā́ti.
lines.en: Thank you so much, doctor. May God keep you happy.

culture: Pashtuns visit the sick (د ناروغ پوښتنه, 'asking after the sick') as a social duty — expect a stream of relatives bringing fruit and good wishes, and blessings like خدای دې شفا درکړي. Many people combine modern medicine with traditional remedies (herbal teas, honey, a trip to a shrine). In conservative families a woman will prefer a female doctor (ډاکټره), and a male relative usually accompanies her. If you have to explain symptoms, pointing and using the body-part words from this unit with درد کوي will get you a long way.

sentences.roman: də haġé stə́rge ḍére ṣkə́le di.

sentences.en: The baby has a little nose.

tip.title: 'My head hurts': the body part is the subject
tip.body:
- Say 'head-my hurts': سر **مې** خوږېږي, or 'head-my pain does': سر مې درد **کوي**.
- The clitic shows whose: **مې** my · **دې** your · **يې** his/her.
- The verb goes with the body part, not with you: always خوږېږي / درد کوي — never خوږېږم.
tip.pattern: body part + مې + خوږېږي / درد کوي

sentences.en: The child has a stomach ache.

sentences.native: احمد جان، څه شوي دي؟ ملا دې خوږېږي؟
sentences.roman: ahmád jān, tsə shə́wi di? mlā de xwaẓéẓi?
sentences.en: Ahmad dear, what's wrong? Does your back hurt?
The children are well, thank God.

tip.title: Saying you're ill
tip.body:
- Fever, cough: use **لرل** 'have': تبه **لرم**, ټوخی **لري**.
- A cold: زکام **شوی** يم (man) / زکام **شوې** يم (woman) 'I've caught a cold'.
- ناروغ 'ill' agrees: زه ناروغ يم (m), زه ناروغ**ه** يم (f).

sentences.en: The children have a fever and a cough.

lessons.title: You should rest

tip.title: 'Should, must': بايد + و- form
tip.body:
- **بايد** never changes; the verb after it takes the **و-** form: بايد استراحت **و**کړم, بايد درمل **و**خورې.
- 'Go' is different: بايد **لاړ شم** 'I must go'.
- 'Shouldn't': **ونه** — بايد **ونه** خورې 'you shouldn't eat (it)'.

new: دا درمل ورځ کې درې ځله وخوره.

sentences.en: Take this medicine morning and evening.
You should rest for two days.

sentences.roman: tso wradzé kéẓi che tabə́ lare?
sentences.en: How many days have you had a fever?
God willing, you'll soon be well.
